processing: Made into rock oolong in the Wuyi manner: partly oxidised, rolled and dried over a roast. The difference from its neighbours lies in the leaf variety rather than in a method of its own.
harvest_season: As with other Wuyi rock teas, a spring picking; no separate prized picking is recorded for this cultivar.
appearance_dry: Dark, twisted strips typical of a roasted Wuyi oolong.
appearance_liquor: A warm reddish amber, clear when well made.
appearance_wet: As with other Wuyi rock teas, open brownish-green leaves that darken towards the edges.
taste_profile: A moderate floral aroma, floral on top, creamy in the middle and fruity at the base.

brewing.notes: Usual rock-tea brewing: a small gaiwan or pot, near-boiling water, short steeps.

vintage_note: Usually sold like other Wuyi rock teas, from the current spring harvest once the roast has rested, often some months after picking. Ask for the harvest year and where it was grown, because the cultivar is made in both the Wuyi and Jian'ou areas and the two need not taste alike.
description:
Ai Jiao Oolong takes its name from the words for short-legged: a Fujian oolong cultivar, sold in English as Short Leg, that you meet today as a Wuyi rock tea and also as a speciality of Jian'ou, a little to the south.

The making follows the general rock-oolong route, and shops that carry it alongside other Wuyi cultivars say the method is shared and the leaf is what differs. Plants moved to Wuyi from elsewhere were observed to keep their growth habit and leaf-edge character while growing somewhat smaller.

In the cup, expect a modest perfume that develops into a floral top, a creamy middle and a fruity base. Brew it as you would other rock teas, near boiling and quick.

Buy it by year and place. Very little is published about grades of this cultivar, so a straightforward statement of harvest and growing area is more useful than any poetic name.
history:
Ai Jiao Oolong is recognised in Fujian as a local oolong cultivar and appears in modern lists of Wuyi varieties. Its origin and the date it was first selected are poorly recorded.

Modern work is mostly agronomic and chemical: a study of cultivars introduced to Wuyi included it, and a food-science paper used Jian'ou samples to describe the flavour of good examples.
